mcqs.q: Salivary secretion occurs in:
opts: Two phases — a primary (acinar) and a secondary (ductal) phase
A single phase in the duct only
mcqs.explain: Saliva forms in a primary phase (secretory acini) and a secondary phase (modification in the ducts).

mcqs.q: The PRIMARY secretion produced by the acini is:
mcqs.explain: Saliva secreted from the acini is isotonic; it becomes hypotonic after ductal modification.

mcqs.q: The acinar cells form saliva by modifying:
opts: Interstitial fluid derived from blood capillaries
mcqs.explain: Fluid arises from interstitial fluid formed from capillary blood, which the acinar cells modify and secrete into the lumen.

mcqs.q: Most ductal modification of saliva occurs in the:
mcqs.explain: Most modification (ion exchange) occurs in the striated ducts, converting isotonic saliva to hypotonic.

mcqs.q: In the ducts, which ions are REABSORBED from saliva?
mcqs.explain: Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are reabsorbed while K⁺ and HCO₃⁻ are secreted, making saliva hypotonic.

mcqs.q: Which ions are SECRETED into saliva in the ducts?
mcqs.explain: Potassium and bicarbonate are secreted while sodium and chloride are reabsorbed during ductal modification.

mcqs.q: As saliva passes through the ductal system it changes from:
mcqs.explain: Ductal ion exchange changes the isotonic acinar secretion into hypotonic saliva.

mcqs.q: The physiologic control of salivary secretion is mediated by the:
mcqs.explain: Salivary secretion is controlled by the autonomic nervous system, plus smell/taste of food and masticatory stimuli.

mcqs.q: Parasympathetic stimulation of the salivary glands:
mcqs.explain: The parasympathetic system increases secretion (watery saliva); the sympathetic system decreases it.

mcqs.q: The dry mouth felt during a 'fight or flight' response is due to:
mcqs.explain: Sympathetic ('fight or flight') activity decreases salivary secretion, producing a dry mouth.

mcqs.q: Hyposalivation (reduced saliva) is clinically called:
mcqs.explain: Reduced salivary secretion (dry mouth) is xerostomia; excess saliva is sialorrhea/ptyalism.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised cause of xerostomia?
opts: Radiation to the gland or drug side effects
mcqs.explain: Xerostomia is caused by destruction of secretory cells (inflammation/radiation), dehydration, psychological causes and drug side effects; teething/cerebral palsy/nausea cause hypersalivation.

mcqs.q: Which drug class commonly causes a dry mouth?
mcqs.explain: Anticholinergics, antidepressants, antipsychotics and antihypertensives interfere with the neuro-regulation of secretion and cause xerostomia.

mcqs.q: A major dental consequence of xerostomia is:
opts: Increased susceptibility to caries and oral infection
mcqs.explain: Reduced saliva makes teeth caries-prone and oral tissues prone to infection, inflammation and ulceration, with difficult speech/chewing/swallowing.

mcqs.q: Excess salivation (sialorrhea) in a pathological condition is also termed:
mcqs.explain: Pathological hypersalivation is known as ptyalism or sialorrhea.

mcqs.q: Which is a recognised cause of sialorrhea?
opts: Teething or neurological disorders (e.g. cerebral palsy)
mcqs.explain: Hypersalivation occurs with acute oral/tongue inflammation, teething, nausea/vomiting, neurological disorders (cerebral palsy) and foreign appliances.

mcqs.q: A foreign object such as a new orthodontic appliance may cause:
mcqs.explain: Any foreign material in the mouth, such as an orthodontic appliance, can stimulate hypersalivation.

mcqs.q: The serous cells of the acinus produce a ___ secretion, and mucous cells produce a ___ secretion:
mcqs.explain: Serous cells produce a watery secretion; mucous cells produce a viscous, mucin-rich secretion.

mcqs.q: Besides the autonomic nerves, salivary secretion is also stimulated by:
opts: The smell/taste of food and masticatory stimuli
mcqs.explain: Secretion is linked to the changing smell or taste of food and to masticatory (chewing) stimuli.

mcqs.q: Why does saliva become hypotonic by the time it reaches the mouth?
opts: More ions (Na⁺/Cl⁻) are reabsorbed than are secreted in the ducts
Water is added in the ducts
mcqs.explain: Net reabsorption of Na⁺ and Cl⁻ (greater than the secretion of K⁺/HCO₃⁻) leaves the final saliva hypotonic.

saqs.q: Describe the two phases of saliva formation.
saqs.a: Primary phase: acini modify interstitial fluid and secrete an isotonic fluid into the lumen. Secondary phase: ductal (mainly striated-duct) modification makes it hypotonic.

saqs.q: Explain the ductal ion exchange that makes saliva hypotonic.
saqs.a: In the striated ducts, Na⁺ and Cl⁻ are reabsorbed while K⁺ and HCO₃⁻ are secreted; net ion loss leaves the saliva hypotonic.

saqs.q: How is salivary secretion regulated by the autonomic nervous system?
saqs.a: Parasympathetic increases secretion (watery saliva); sympathetic decreases it (dry mouth of 'fight or flight'). Smell/taste and chewing also stimulate secretion.

saqs.q: Define xerostomia and list its causes.
saqs.a: Reduced saliva (hyposalivation). Causes: destruction of secretory cells (inflammation/radiation), dehydration, psychological (anxiety/depression), and drugs (anticholinergics, antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihypertensives).

saqs.q: What are the effects of xerostomia?
saqs.a: Difficulty in speech, mastication, taste and swallowing; teeth become caries-prone; oral tissues prone to infection, inflammation and ulceration.

saqs.q: Define sialorrhea and list its causes.
saqs.a: Excess saliva (hypersalivation/ptyalism). Causes: acute mouth/tongue inflammation, teething, nausea/vomiting, neurological disorders (cerebral palsy), foreign material (orthodontic appliance).

saqs.q: Contrast serous and mucous acinar secretions.
saqs.a: Serous cells produce a watery secretion (enzymes); mucous cells produce a viscous, mucin-rich secretion.
